title: Tushin's Battery
text:
In War and Peace, Tolstoy describes the battle of Schongrabern in 1805, where a small Russian rearguard under Prince Bagration had to hold off the French. In the middle of the line stood a battery of four guns commanded by Captain Tushin, a small, shy, awkward officer with a pipe, whom his superiors barely noticed.

In the confusion of the battle, Tushin's battery was simply forgotten. No infantry covered it. Nobody told him what to do. So he decided for himself to fire on the village of Schongrabern in front of him, and the village caught fire. The flames and the steady fire of his guns slowed the French advance, and the French, seeing so much resistance, assumed a large force was there.

Tushin's gunners worked under heavy fire, losing men and horses, while Tushin, half dreaming, imagined his guns as living creatures and himself as a giant hurling cannonballs. His men loved him. When at last Prince Andrei rode up with orders to withdraw, he found them still firing, and he helped bring the guns away.

That evening, at Bagration's headquarters, a staff officer complained that Tushin had abandoned two guns. Tushin stood there tongue-tied, unable to defend himself. It was Prince Andrei who spoke up: the day's success, he said, was owed above all to Tushin's battery and its men.
lesson: The people who decide a result are often the quiet ones doing their job without being seen. Make sure the credit reaches them, and speak up when it does not.
people: Captain Tushin, his gunners, Prince Andrei Bolkonsky, Prince Bagration
source: Leo Tolstoy, War and Peace, Volume I, Part 2, chapters 20 to 21
caveat: Schongrabern was a real battle, but Tushin and his role are Tolstoy's fiction.
